title: Yonsei University to Upgrade On-Premises IBM Quantum System One to Next-Generation Nighthawk QPU - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Yonsei University will swap its on-premises 127-qubit IBM Eagle QPU for IBM's 120-qubit Nighthawk in November 2026 — fewer qubits but a square lattice with 4 neighbors per qubit via 218 tunable couplers, claimed to yield ~40% more computational throughput at equal fidelity by eliminating SWAP gates, and paired with a Fugaku hybrid workflow for Leigh syndrome drug research.

insights.claim: Yonsei University will replace its 127-qubit IBM Eagle QPU with IBM's 120-qubit Nighthawk in November 2026 — a downgrade in raw qubit count that is marketed as an upgrade in capability.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Qubit count is now formally a misleading headline metric; screen quantum claims on connectivity, gate depth and error rates instead.

insights.claim: Nighthawk's square lattice gives each qubit 4 direct connections via 218 tunable couplers, versus roughly 2.5 average neighbors under Eagle's heavy-hex layout.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Coupler count and connectivity degree are the specs to track in superconducting roadmaps; they determine how much of a circuit is wasted on routing.
insights.quote: gives each qubit 4 direct connections via 218 tunable couplers.

insights.claim: Quadrupling adjacent connectivity eliminates a substantial number of intermediate SWAP gates, reducing gate depth overhead and enabling roughly 40% more computational throughput at equivalent fidelity levels.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A 40% throughput gain from topology alone, with no fidelity improvement, shows architecture changes can substitute for hard physics progress — cheaper and faster to ship.
insights.quote: reducing gate depth overhead and enabling ~40% more computational throughput at equivalent fidelity levels.

insights.claim: Yonsei will be only the second facility globally to host a Nighthawk-based quantum computer, after IBM Miami.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Nighthawk's installed base is currently two sites — the rollout pace of this generation is the real measure of IBM's manufacturing capacity claims.
insights.quote: making Yonsei the second facility globally—after IBM Miami—to host a Nighthawk-based quantum computer.

insights.claim: Yonsei is running its QPU in a hybrid workflow with RIKEN's Fugaku supercomputer in Japan to study target mechanisms for Leigh syndrome, a severe genetic neurological disorder.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Cross-border Korea-Japan compute sharing on a live biomedical target is a template for how quantum capacity gets pooled without exporting hardware.

insights.claim: The hybrid division of labor uses the QPU to filter key chemical candidate spaces before offloading heavy processing to classical HPC, a pattern projected to compress simulation timelines from decades to days.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Quantum as a candidate-space filter feeding classical compute is the practical near-term architecture — value accrues to the orchestration layer, not just the QPU.
insights.quote: is projected to compress long-term simulation timelines from decades to days.

insights.claim: Yonsei is forming dual research nodes with the University of Cambridge's Milner Therapeutics Institute to apply Nighthawk-based quantum algorithms to AI-driven drug discovery and stem cell research.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Academic node networks are how quantum algorithms reach pharma pipelines; these partnerships front-run commercial licensing deals.
insights.locator: The initiative is also forming dual research nodes

insights.claim: Alongside the November QPU installation Yonsei will launch Q-Bridge, a quantum-classical integration software platform, plus a Q-Library domain-specific algorithm repository so non-quantum enterprise partners can input industrial data and execute hybrid algorithms.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on quantum adoption is the absence of domain algorithm libraries, not hardware — software abstraction layers are where the defensible margin may sit.

insights.claim: On-premises IBM Quantum System One installations at national universities are functioning as sovereign compute assets, with Yonsei's Songdo campus facility anchoring South Korea's national quantum initiative.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Sovereign quantum procurement is a durable, price-insensitive demand channel for IBM — government budgets, not enterprise ROI, underwrite the current installed base.
insights.locator: The Yonsei Quantum Initiative at Yonsei University
